# Toast at four

I haven’t written here since spring. I thought that, when the time came, this post would be easy. It hasn’t been. Every attempt so far has turned into either a eulogy for night shifts or a complaint about the NHS, and I don’t want to write either. So I’ll try to keep it plain.

On Saturday 7 November 2026, I worked my last night shift: 21:00 to 07:30, in majors. After fourteen years of nights, I start a days-only rota on Monday.

There isn’t one dramatic reason. My knees have views on the stairs. My sleep has become something I negotiate with rather than something I do. And my GP recently made it clear that my blood pressure is not a joke any more. At 42, I have finally reached the stage of taking seriously the sort of boring, sensible advice I have been giving other people for years.

It is the right decision. I am relieved about it.

I am also surprisingly not okay.

My first nights were as an SHO in 2012. During that first winter, I sat in my car in the car park at the Infirmary and cried because I couldn’t remember whether I had given a second dose. I had. I established that I had, and still couldn’t make myself feel certain enough to drive away. I can still remember the frost on the windscreen, and sitting there with the engine off, trying to work out how everyone else appeared to know what they were doing.

They didn’t, of course. Not always. That was one of the first useful things nights taught me: competence and certainty are not the same thing. You can be careful, competent and still frightened. You can check something three times and need to check it once more. You can ask for help without that being the moment everyone discovers you should never have been allowed through the door.

Nights gave me an education I wouldn’t have chosen in that form, but wouldn’t now want to give back.

People think they are mostly about adrenaline. Sometimes they are. Mostly, though, they are about staying kind at 5am when you are empty. Kind when your patience has gone, your thoughts have slowed, and somebody needs something explained again. Kind to the person who has apologised for bothering you. Kind to the colleague who has made a mistake. Kind to yourself, if there is any left over, which there often isn’t.

I have not always managed it. But nights made me better at recognising when somebody was running on nothing, including me.

They are also where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers, more honesty and, often, more kindness. Not because the people at night are better than the people during the day, but because there is less energy available for pretence. At three in the morning, you find out fairly quickly who will make you a cup of tea without being asked, who will quietly take the next task off your list, and who will tell you the truth in a way that lets you do something useful with it.

Folasade, our charge nurse, has done nights for 22 years and still beats me up the stairs. This used to be merely annoying. Now that my knees have joined the conversation, it feels almost personal. She has seen every kind of night, every kind of confidence and panic, and has an uncanny ability to make a difficult situation feel workable without pretending that it isn’t difficult.

And then there is the toast.

Somebody always makes toast in the staff room at four in the morning. Nobody admits to starting it. There is no rota, no origin story, no official announcement. Bread goes into the toaster and then there is toast. Sometimes that small, ordinary smell is the first thing in hours that makes the world seem properly anchored. It is difficult not to love a tradition that nobody owns.

Last winter, at around three in the morning, an elderly gentleman held my hand and told me that I had his daughter’s hands. He went home three days later. It wasn’t a dramatic moment. Nothing needed doing because of it. We simply sat with it for a few seconds before the night carried on.

Those are the moments I have found hardest to explain to people who don’t work nights. Not the big rescues or the noisy emergencies, but the brief, unpolished human exchanges that happen when everybody is tired and there is very little performance left. Nights gave me a great many of those. They also gave me colleagues who have seen me unsure, bad-tempered, frightened, amused at inappropriate moments, and occasionally eating toast as though it were a clinical intervention.

But if I write only that, this becomes the eulogy I’m trying to avoid.

Nights took sleep. They took ordinary weekends and the ability to say yes to things without first consulting a rota. They took mornings when I was technically present but not much use to anybody. They took the simple pleasure of waking up and knowing, roughly, what time it was without having to reconstruct the previous twelve hours.

Because of nights, both of my nieces’ naming ceremonies came to me over video, which is another way of saying that I missed them. My sister, in Bangalore, never once complained. Not once. She was loving and understanding and made it as easy as she could. That generosity doesn’t mean nothing was lost. It just means she helped me carry it.

I don’t want to turn any of this into martyrdom. Plenty of people work unsociable hours; plenty miss things that matter. But changing rotas doesn’t magically return what was missed, and pretending otherwise would be another way of not telling the truth. Nights were good to me in some ways and costly in others. Both things get to be true. There is no requirement to decide which one wins.

On Sunday morning, I drove home down London Road with the sun coming up and Radio 4’s shipping forecast on catch-up. London Road is under no obligation to be poetic at that time of day, and usually isn’t. There are traffic lights and buses and people who have slept at sensible hours. But I have always loved that particular homecoming light: pale, slightly unreal, falling across a city that is starting its day while I am finishing mine.

Halfway home, I realised I would not see that light from this side again.

That caught me more than leaving the department had. Not because I wanted to turn round and do another shift. I absolutely did not. That is the confusing part. You can be finished with something, properly finished, and still grieve the fact that a whole way of living has quietly become the past tense.

I feel like a traitor for being relieved. As if being worn down were proof of loyalty, and wanting to sleep at night were a small betrayal of the people still there. It isn’t, of course. Choosing not to damage myself further is not a judgement on anybody who stays. There is no correct number of nights a person owes.

Fourteen years is simply the number I did.

So this is not an argument for nights, and it isn’t an escape story. It is a thank-you with some bruises in it. I loved parts of that life. I am glad to be leaving it. I will miss the honesty, the odd intimacy, the sunrise from the wrong direction, and the people who knew exactly who I was at 3:40 in the morning.

Tonight, the department will hand itself over again. Somebody will be new and convinced that everyone else knows what they’re doing. Somebody will be running on empty and trying not to show it. Folasade will, in all likelihood, still be beating younger people up the stairs.

And at four o’clock, somebody will make toast.

Nobody will announce it. Nobody will ask who started it. A plate will be pushed towards whoever looks most in need of it, and for a few minutes they can sit down, eat something warm, and not be empty entirely on their own.
